intro: One PNG in, one JPG out at the same pixel dimensions. Transparent areas are filled with white unless you choose black or a colour of your own.
answer: A photograph saved as a PNG stores every pixel exactly and is many times heavier than it needs to be; turning it into a JPG keeps the same picture at the same dimensions but stores it with compression built for photographs, usually for a fraction of the bytes. On Resizo the pair is already fixed at PNG to JPEG, so you add the PNG and press Convert to JPEG. Anything transparent is filled in, because a JPG has no transparency to keep — white by default, since that is what a logo or a signature meets on the page it is going onto, with black and a colour of your own a click away. The whole conversion is done by your own device on codecs the page downloads, so the file never leaves it.

paragraphs: One PNG in, one JPG out at the same pixel dimensions. Transparent areas are filled with white unless you choose black or a colour of your own.
PNG→ to JPEG
JPEG cannot store transparency, so the see-through parts of your image are filled with this colour.
PNG · up to 20 MB

A photograph saved as a PNG stores every pixel exactly and is many times heavier than it needs to be; turning it into a JPG keeps the same picture at the same dimensions but stores it with compression built for photographs, usually for a fraction of the bytes. On Resizo the pair is already fixed at PNG to JPEG, so you add the PNG and press Convert to JPEG. Anything transparent is filled in, because a JPG has no transparency to keep — white by default, since that is what a logo or a signature meets on the page it is going onto, with black and a colour of your own a click away. The whole conversion is done by your own device on codecs the page downloads, so the file never leaves it.
Accepts PNG. Saves JPEG.

PNG is lossless. It stores every pixel exactly as it was and shrinks the file by spotting repetition — runs of identical colour, rows that look like the row above. A screenshot of a spreadsheet is full of that. A photograph has almost none of it, so a photo saved as a PNG is close to storing the raw pixels.

JPEG works the other way round. It throws away the detail your eye tracks least closely, which is exactly the fine random variation a photograph is made of. That is why the same picture can go from above 20 MB to under 2 MB with no visible change at normal viewing size.

This is the one thing to check before you convert. A PNG can carry an alpha channel — the per-pixel record of what is see-through. JPEG has no such channel and no way to represent it, so the transparency has to be filled in with something, and here that something is white.

For a photograph it makes no difference: there is nothing transparent to fill. For a logo or a signature it is usually the right answer, because the form, the document or the slide it is going onto is white already and the fill lands invisibly. Black is one click away for the opposite case — a pale mark, or artwork meant for a dark page.

What the fill cannot do is come back. Once the JPG is written those pixels are opaque for good, so artwork that has to sit on some other colour later should go to WebP instead, which keeps the alpha channel and still lands well under the PNG.

The PNG is decoded back to raw pixels and written out again as a JPEG at quality 80 — the setting most of the web uses as its default. Width and height are untouched, so a 1920×1080 PNG is a 1920×1080 JPG. Nothing is cropped, scaled or rotated.

The download keeps the original name inside a Resizo prefix, so logo.png comes back as resizo-converted-logo.jpg. EXIF and GPS metadata are absent from the JPG, and the whole thing happens on your own device: the file is read, converted and saved where it already was, and none of it is transmitted.

It adds one generation of lossy compression, written here at quality 80. On a photograph that is very hard to see at normal viewing size. On a screenshot full of small text, or a flat graphic with hard edges, it is much easier to spot — those are the files worth keeping as PNG.

JPEG has no alpha channel, so transparency cannot survive the conversion. Every transparent pixel has to be filled in, and the fill is white unless you say otherwise, because most of what comes through here is headed for a white page. The “Transparent areas become” control above the button switches it to black or to any colour you name — other converters hand you black without asking, which is where a mark on a black rectangle comes from. If the transparency itself matters, convert the PNG to WebP instead, which keeps the alpha channel and is still smaller than the PNG.

It depends entirely on the picture. A 12-megapixel photograph saved as a PNG can sit above 20 MB and usually comes back under 2 MB as a JPG. A flat graphic with a handful of colours is the opposite case: PNG already stores it efficiently, and the JPG can come out no smaller, or even slightly larger.

You can, and the file will be a valid PNG, but it will not undo anything. The detail JPEG discarded is gone, and the PNG faithfully stores the compressed result — usually at several times the size. Keep the original PNG if you might need it again.

One PNG per pass, up to 20 MB, and 8000 pixels on the longest side. The pixel dimensions are never changed by this tool — if you also need the image smaller on screen, resize it first and then convert.

Yes — this page uploads nothing. The PNG decoder and the JPEG encoder are downloaded into the tab as code the first time you use it, and from then on your file is read, converted and saved by your own machine. PNGs are very often screenshots, which is exactly the kind of file you would rather not hand to a stranger, and this one goes nowhere. The JPG is written from raw pixels and carries no EXIF or GPS data.

Screenshots with text in them. JPEG smears the sharp black-on-white edges of letterforms, and small type is where it shows first.
